cues.text: ODYSSEY — BOOK XIV
The hut of Eumaeus: the slave's welcome, the second Cretan tale, the cloak story.
But he went up from the harbor by a rough track\nthrough wooded country, along the heights, where Athena
had shown him the noble swineherd — the man who cared
for his substance beyond all the\nhouse-slaves noble Odysseus had acquired.
He found him sitting in the fore-court, where his yard
was built up high, in a place\nwith a clear view all around,
big and handsome, with a cleared\nrun round it. The swineherd
had built it himself for the swine of his absent master —\nwithout his mistress, without old Laertes —
out of quarried stones, and coped it with wild pear;
and outside he had driven stakes the\nwhole circuit, this way and that,
close-set and thick, split out of the black heart of\nthe oak; and inside the yard he had made twelve sties
hard by one another, bedding for the swine;\nand in each one fifty wallowing sows were penned,
breeding females. The boars slept outside,\nfar fewer: for the godlike suitors kept thinning them
at their feasts — the swineherd forever\nsending in the best of all the fatted hogs;
and these numbered three hundred and sixty.
And beside them four dogs always slept — like wild\nbeasts, raised by the swineherd, a leader of men.
He himself was fitting sandals to his feet,\ncutting them from a well-tanned oxhide. The others
had gone their ways, this man here,\nthat man there, with the herded swine —
three of them; the fourth he had sent off to the city
to bring a hog to the overweening suitors — forced to it —
so they might slaughter it and\nglut their hearts with meat.
Suddenly the baying dogs caught sight of Odysseus:
they rushed him, yelping. And Odysseus sat down —\npure craft — and the staff dropped from his hand.
There, at his own farm,\nhe would have suffered shameful hurt,
but the swineherd came fast on his quick feet after them,
darting through the gateway —\nthe hide flew from his hand —
and shouting he scattered the dogs this way and that\nwith a shower of stones. And he addressed his master:
"Old man — the dogs came one breath short of tearing you
to pieces, and the shame of it would have poured on me.
And the gods have given me griefs\nenough besides, and groaning:
here I sit, mourning a godlike master,\nand fatten hogs for other men
to eat, while he, perhaps, is starving for bread and\nwanders the lands and towns of men of alien speech —
if indeed he lives still, and sees the light of the sun.
But follow me — into the hut, old man, so that you too,\nwhen you have had your fill of bread and wine,
may say where you come from,\nand all the cares you have borne."
So speaking the noble swineherd led him to the hut,
brought him in and set him down:\nhe heaped springy brushwood
and spread on it the skin of a shaggy wild goat —\nhis own bedding, big and thick. And Odysseus was glad
that he received him so, and spoke a word, and named him:
"May Zeus grant you, stranger,\nand the other deathless gods,
whatever you wish most — since you\nwelcomed me with all your heart."
And you answered him, Eumaeus the swineherd:
"Stranger, it is not right for me —\nnot though a worse man came —
to slight a stranger:\nfor from Zeus they come, all of them,
strangers and beggars; and a gift, though small, is dear —
from such as we are: for that is the way of slaves,\nalways afraid, when the masters who hold the power
are the young ones. As for him —\nthe gods have bound his homecoming,
the man who would have loved me devotedly,\nand given me possessions —
a house, a plot of land,\na wife that many men had courted —
such things as a kind-hearted master gives his house-slave
who has labored hard for him,\nwhose work a god makes prosper,
the way this work of mine prospers,\nat which I hold my post.
For that my master would have paid\nme richly, had he grown old here.
But he is dead. — And I wish\nHelen's whole breed had gone down
on its knees to destruction,\nfor she loosed the knees of many men:
he too went off for the sake of Agamemnon's honor\nto Ilium of the fine horses, to fight the Trojans."
So speaking he quickly belted in his tunic with his sash
and went to the sties, where the\ntribes of young pigs were penned.
He took two out of there, and slaughtered them both,
singed them, cut them small, and threaded them on spits,
and when he had roasted all of it,\nhe brought and set it by Odysseus
hot on the spits themselves,\nand dusted it with white barley,
and mixed honey-sweet wine in an ivy-wood bowl,\nand sat down facing him, and pressed him on:
"Eat now, stranger — what house-slaves have to offer:
young pig. The fatted hogs — the suitors eat those,
with no thought in their hearts of\nthe gods' watching eye, no mercy.
Yet the blessed gods love no ruthless dealing:
they honor justice, and the right acts of men.
Why — even enemies, even raiders, who land on\na foreign coast, and Zeus grants them plunder,
and they fill their ships and set off home — even on\ntheir hearts falls the strong fear of the watching eye.
But these men — these men know something;\nthey have heard some god's own voice
telling his grim death: that is why they will not woo
in the right way, nor go home\nto their own, but at their ease
they devour the goods, high-handed, and spare nothing.
For every night and every day that comes from Zeus,\nthey slaughter victims — never one, and never only two —
and wine they draw off past all measure, and waste it.
For his livelihood was past speaking. No hero\nanywhere had so much — not on the dark mainland,
not on Ithaca itself; no twenty men together have\nwealth so great. I will count it through for you:
twelve herds of cattle on the mainland;\nas many flocks of sheep;
as many droves of pigs; as many ranging herds of goats
in the care of foreigners and of his own herdsmen there.
And here, at the island's end, wide-ranging herds of goats
graze, eleven in all, with good men watching over them,
and every day each man of them\ndrives up a beast for those others —
whichever of the fatted goats looks best;\nand I keep guard over these sows, and protect them,
and choose out the best of the swine, and send it in."
So he spoke; and Odysseus ate his meat and drank his wine,
ravenous, silent — planting evils for the suitors.
But when he had supped, and steadied his heart with food,\nthe swineherd filled the cup he drank from himself
brim-full of wine and gave it;\nand he took it, glad at heart,
and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to him:
"Friend — who was the man who bought you with his goods,\nthe master rich and powerful as you describe?
You say he perished for the sake of Agamemnon's honor:
name him — I may know him, being such a one as he was.
For Zeus knows, I suppose, and the other deathless gods,
whether I have seen him. I have wandered far."
Then the swineherd answered him, a leader of men:
"Old man — no wanderer coming with news of him\ncould persuade his wife now, or his dear son.
Drifters in need of keep — they lie at random,\nand have no wish to speak the truth.
Every vagrant who finds his way to the land of\nIthaca goes to my mistress and babbles his deceits;
and she receives him kindly,\nand treats him well, and questions everything,
and as she grieves the tears come falling from her lids,
as is the right way of a wife whose husband dies far off.
You too, old man, would have a\nstory stitched together fast enough
if someone would give you clothing — a cloak and a tunic.
But him — by now the dogs and the quick birds
have torn the skin from his bones,\nand the life has gone out of him;
or the fish have eaten him in the sea, and his bones
lie on a shore somewhere, wrapped deep in drifting sand.
So he is dead and gone over there,\nand grief is left behind
for all who loved him — for me above all: for never\nagain will I find a master so gentle, wherever I go —
not though I came again to my father's and my mother's\nhouse, where I was born, and where they reared me.
And it is not even for them I\nmourn so much, for all my longing
to see them with my eyes again in my own country:
no — it is longing for Odysseus,\nwho is gone, that takes hold of me.
I shrink from naming him, stranger, even now he is absent,
for he loved me beyond measure, and cared for me at heart.
I call him 'my beloved lord,' even far away."
Then much-enduring noble Odysseus spoke to him again:
"Friend — since you deny it flat, and say that he will\ncome no more, and your heart is set in disbelief —
then I will say it not just so, but with an oath upon it:
Odysseus is coming home. And let my reward for the\ngood news come the moment he arrives at his own halls:
dress me then in a cloak and a tunic, fine clothing.
Before that — though I stand in\nsore need — I will take nothing.
For hateful to me as the very gates of Hades is\nthe man who yields to poverty and babbles deceits.
Now Zeus be my witness, first of the gods,\nand this table of friendship,
and the hearth of blameless Odysseus,\nto which I have come:
all this shall be accomplished exactly as I say.
Within this very turning of the\nlight Odysseus will be here:
between this month's waning and the rising of the next,\nhe will come home; and he will punish whoever
dishonors his wife and his shining son in this place."
And you answered him, Eumaeus the swineherd:
"Old man, I will never be paying\nthat reward for good news,
and Odysseus will come home no more. Drink your wine
in peace, and let us turn our\nminds to other things. Do not
remind me of all this: for the heart in my breast\naches whenever anyone recalls my faithful master.
As for the oath — we will let it be. But may\nOdysseus come — as I wish it, as Penelope wishes,
and old Laertes, and godlike Telemachus.
And now it is the boy I mourn\nwithout ceasing — Odysseus' own son
Telemachus. The gods reared him like a young tree,\nand I thought he would stand among men no whit behind
his own dear father, a wonder in build and beauty —\nand some immortal crippled the balanced mind within him,
or some man did: he has gone for news of his father\nto holy Pylos. And the lordly suitors lie in wait
for his homecoming — so that the line of godlike\nArceisius may perish out of Ithaca and leave no name.
Well — we will let him be, whether he is taken or escapes,\nand the son of Cronos stretches a hand over him.
But come, old man, tell me your own troubles now;\nand tell me this too, honestly, so that I may know it:
What man are you, and from where?\nWhere are your city and your parents?
On what kind of ship did you come? And how did\nsailors bring you to Ithaca? Who did they claim to be?
For I hardly think you came here on foot."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered him:
"Then I will tell you all of it, and truly.
If only there were food for the two of us,\nfor a good while, and sweet wine here inside the hut,
to feast on quietly while others did the work —\nthen I could go on easily for a full year
and still not finish out the tale of my heart's cares,\nall that I have labored through by the gods' will.
Out of wide Crete I claim my lineage:
a rich man's son. Many other sons besides\nwere born and bred in his hall, true-born,
sons of his wife. My mother was bought — a concubine.
Yet Castor, Hylax' son — the man whose blood I claim —\nhonored me equally with his lawful sons.
In those days the Cretan people honored him like a god\nfor his fortune, his wealth, and his glorious sons.
But the death-spirits came and carried him away\nto the house of Hades. And his high-hearted sons
divided up the living and cast lots for it,\nand to me they gave a pittance, and allotted me a house.
Still, I won myself a wife from a family of wide\nholdings — by my own worth: for I was no empty man,
no shirker of the fight. Now it is all gone from me;\nbut even so, I think, looking at the stubble
you can tell the standing grain. Since then,\ntrouble past measure has held me.
Ares and Athena, yes, they gave me boldness and the\nstrength that breaks men's ranks. Whenever I picked
the best men for an ambush, sowing evils for the enemy,\nmy proud heart never once looked forward to death:
far the first, I would leap out\nand take my man with the spear —
whichever of the enemy gave me his back in flight.
Such I was in war. But field-work I never loved,\nnor the housekeeping that rears shining children:
what I loved, always, was the oared ships,\nand wars, and polished javelins, and arrows —
grim things, that other men shudder at.
But I loved what the god, I suppose, set in my heart:
one man delights in one work, another in another.
For before the sons of the Achaeans set foot on Troy,\nnine times I led men and fast-running ships
against foreign peoples, and rich takings came my way.
From it I drew out my pleasure, and much fell to me
by lot besides. My house grew great at once,\nand thereafter I walked among the Cretans feared and respected.
But when Zeus of the wide voice devised at last\nthat hateful road that loosed the knees of many men,
then they pressed me and glorious Idomeneus to\nlead the ships to Ilium. There was no device
for refusing: the people's hard talk held us to it.
There we sons of the Achaeans made war nine years,\nand in the tenth we sacked Priam's city and set off
home with our ships; and a god scattered the Achaeans.
But for me — wretched me —\nZeus the deviser designed evils.
One month, no more, I stayed, delighting in my children,\nmy wedded wife, and my possessions. And then
my heart bade me fit out ships and sail\nfor Egypt, with my godlike companions.
Nine ships I fitted out, and the crews gathered fast.
Six days after that my trusted companions\nfeasted, and I gave victims in plenty
for sacrifice to the gods,\nand for the men to make their feast.
On the seventh we boarded, and from wide Crete\nwe sailed with a fresh fair North Wind behind us,
easily, as if downstream. No ship\nof mine took harm: unhurt and whole
we sat, and the wind and the\nsteersmen held them on course.
On the fifth day we reached the\nfair-flowing river of Egypt,
and in the river of Egypt I moored my curved ships.
Then, you may be sure, I ordered my trusted companions\nto stay there by the ships and guard the ships,
and I sent out scouts to the lookout places.
But they gave way to arrogance —\nfollowed their own force —
and straightway began to pillage the beautiful fields
of the Egyptian men: they carried\noff the women and small children,
and killed the men. And quickly the cry reached the city.
Hearing the shout, at the showing of dawn the people
came; and the whole plain filled with infantry and horses
and the lightning of bronze.\nAnd Zeus who delights in thunder
threw an evil panic on my companions, and no man dared
stand and face it: for destruction ringed us everywhere.
There they killed many of us with the sharp bronze,
and others they led up alive, to slave for them by force.
But as for me — Zeus himself put this thought in\nmy mind (would I had died instead, and met my doom
there, in Egypt! for more grief\nstood waiting to receive me):
at once I took the well-made helmet from my head,
and the shield from my shoulders,\nand dropped the spear from my hand,
and went straight toward the king's chariot,
and clasped his knees and kissed them.\nHe spared me, and had mercy,
and sat me in his car, and took me, weeping, to his house.
Truly, man after man came\nlunging at me with the ash spear,
raging to kill me — for they\nwere angered beyond all measure —
but he held them off: he feared the wrath of Zeus of\nStrangers, who above all feels fury at evil deeds.
There I stayed seven years, and I gathered much\nwealth among the Egyptian men: for all of them gave.
But when the eighth year came wheeling round for me,
then there came a Phoenician,\na man well-schooled in deceits —
a gnawer of men, who had already done the world much harm.
He talked me round, that one, and took me with him to\nPhoenicia, where his house and his possessions lay,
and there I stayed with him for the full round of a year.
But when at last the months and the\ndays were coming to fulfillment,
as the year rolled round and the seasons came again,\nhe put me aboard a seagoing ship for Libya —
a lying scheme: I was to help him run a cargo there,
but there he meant to sell me, and take a boundless price.
I went with him aboard — suspecting it, but forced.
And she ran on with a fresh fair North Wind behind her,
on the mid-sea track above Crete.\nAnd Zeus was devising their destruction:
for when we had left Crete behind,\nand no other land showed anywhere — only sky and sea —
then the son of Cronos set a dark-blue cloud over\nthe hollow ship, and the deep went black beneath it.
And Zeus thundered in the same instant,\nand hurled his bolt into the ship,
and she shivered stem to stern,\nstruck by the bolt of Zeus,
and filled with the reek of sulfur;\nand all the men fell from the ship.
Like sea-crows around the black hull
they were carried off on the waves;\nand the god took away their homecoming.
But as for me — Zeus himself,\nthough my heart was full of anguish,
put the huge mast of the dark-blue-prowed ship into\nmy two hands, so that I might yet escape the evil.
Wrapped around it I was carried before the deadly winds.
Nine days I was carried;\nand on the tenth, in the black night,
a great rolling wave brought\nme near the Thesprotians' land.
There the king of the Thesprotians, the hero Pheidon,\ntook me in — and asked no price: his own dear son
had found me beaten down by cold\nand weariness, and led me home,
raising me up by the hand,\nuntil we reached his father's halls;
and he put clothing on me, a cloak and a tunic.
It was there I heard of Odysseus. For the king said
he had hosted him, a guest and friend,\non his way home to his fathers' land,
and he showed me all the treasure Odysseus had gathered —\nbronze and gold and iron worked with labor —
enough to feed a man's line to the tenth generation,\nsuch a store of it lay in the lord's halls.
Odysseus, he said, was gone to Dodona, to hear the\nwill of Zeus out of the god's own high-crowned oak:
how he should come home to the rich land of Ithaca,\nopenly or in secret, after so long away.
And he swore an oath to me,\npouring the libation in his house,
that a ship was hauled down and a crew standing\nready to convey him home to his own dear fatherland.
But me he sent off first: for a Thesprotian ship\nhappened to be sailing for Dulichium, rich in wheat.
He charged them to bring me there,\nwith all care, to King Acastus.
But an evil counsel about me\npleased their hearts instead —
so that I might yet come down to the last dregs of misery.
When the seagoing ship was far out from the land,
they set about contriving,\nthen and there, my day of slavery.
They stripped me of my clothing, cloak and tunic both,\nand threw around me different gear — this foul rag
and this torn tunic — the very\nones you see with your own eyes;
and at evening they reached the\ntilled fields of clear-skied Ithaca.
There they lashed me tight in the well-benched ship\nwith a twisted rope, and went ashore themselves
and hurried their supper along the margin of the sea.
But the gods themselves undid my lashing —\neasily. And wrapping my rag about my head,
I slid down the polished lading-plank, breasted the sea,\nthen struck out with both arms, swimming,
and very soon I was out of the water, clear of them.
I climbed up where a thicket of flowering brush stood,\nand lay there, crouched. And they, groaning loud,
cast about; but there seemed no profit for them\nin searching further, so they went back again
aboard their hollow ship. And the gods hid me easily,\nand brought me on my way to the steading
of an understanding man.\nFor it is still my portion to live."
And you answered him, Eumaeus the swineherd:
"Poor luckless stranger —\ntruly you have stirred the heart in me,
telling all this through, all you\nhave suffered, all your wandering.
But one part is not in order,\nand you will never persuade me —
that about Odysseus. Why should a man like you\nlie into the empty air? I know it well myself,
my master's homecoming: how the gods all hated him,
utterly — since they did not\nbring him down among the Trojans,
or in the arms of his friends,\nonce he had wound the war to its end.
Then the whole Achaean people would have built him a tomb,
and he would have won great fame in\ntime to come for his son as well.
Instead the whirlwinds have\nsnatched him away without glory.
And I — I keep apart, with my pigs. I do not go to\nthe city, unless perhaps watchful-minded Penelope
bids me come, when news arrives from somewhere;
then they all sit around the newcomer and question\neverything — those who grieve for their long-gone lord,
and those who rejoice, eating up his living unpunished.
But I have no love of asking and inquiring,\never since an Aetolian cheated me with his tale —
a man who had killed someone,\nand wandered over the wide earth,
and came to my house; and I received him with open arms.
He said he had seen him among\nthe Cretans, at Idomeneus' side,
mending the ships the storms had shattered on him,\nand said he would come by summer, or by harvest-time,
bringing much wealth,\ntogether with his godlike companions.
So you, old man of many sorrows —\nsince some power has brought you to me —
do not court my favor with lies, do not charm me:
it is not for that I will respect you or befriend you,
And out of pity for yourself."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered him:
"Truly the heart in your breast is past all persuading —
such a man you are: not even my oath\nwon you over; nothing convinces you.
Come then, let us make a bargain\nof it — and above the two of us
let the gods who hold Olympus stand witness on both sides.
If your master comes home, to this very house,\nyou dress me in a cloak and a tunic, and send me on
to Dulichium, where my own heart longs to be;\nand if your master does not come as I say he will,
set your slaves on me: pitch me down from the great rock —
so that the next beggar too may\nthink twice before he cheats."
And the noble swineherd answered him, and said:
"Stranger — and a fine name I would win among\nmankind for goodness, now and ever after,
I who led you to my hut and gave you a guest's due,\nif then I killed you and took the dear life out of you:
with a clean heart, after that,\nI could pray to Zeus the son of Cronos!
But it is supper time. Soon now my companions should\nbe in, so we can make a savory supper in the hut."
So the two of them spoke such things to one another;\nand the swine came near, and the men who herd them.
They shut the sows in their pens for the night's sleep,
and a clamor past speech went up as the swine were folded.
Then the noble swineherd called to his companions:
"Bring the best of the hogs,\nso I may slaughter it for a guest
from far away. And we will have some good of it ourselves,
who bear the misery of these\nwhite-tusked swine and suffer for it
so long, while others eat our labor and pay nothing."
So speaking, he split the\nfirewood with the pitiless bronze,
and they brought in a hog, well fattened, five years old,\nand stood it by the hearth. Nor did the swineherd
forget the deathless ones: for his mind was set on good.
No — beginning the rite,\nhe cast into the fire the head-bristles
of the white-tusked hog, and prayed to all the gods\nthat wise Odysseus might come home to his own house.
Then he lifted an oak billet,\nleft over from the splitting,
and struck: and the life left the hog;\nand the others cut the throat,
and singed it, and quickly\nquartered it out. And the swineherd,
beginning the offering, laid raw flesh from every\nlimb in the rich fat, and cast the pieces in the fire,
sprinkled over with barley meal; and they carved the rest
and threaded it on spits, and roasted it with care,
and drew it all off, and heaped it\non the platters. And the swineherd
stood up to divide it: for his mind knew what was fair.
Into seven portions he divided the whole:
one he set aside, with a prayer,\nfor the Nymphs and for Hermes,
Maia's son; the rest he served out to each man;\nand Odysseus he honored with the long unbroken chine
of the white-tusked hog —\nand made his master's heart proud.
And Odysseus of the many designs\nlifted his voice and said:
"Eumaeus — may you be as dear to father Zeus
as you are to me: for you honor such\na man as I am now with the best."
And you answered him, Eumaeus the swineherd:
"Eat, my god-touched guest,\nand take your pleasure in such things
as are here. The god will give\none thing and let another go,
whatever his own heart wills: for he can do all things."
He spoke, and burned the first-cuts\nto the gods who are forever,
and poured the fire-bright wine,\nand set the cup in the hands
of Odysseus, sacker of cities;\nand sat down to his own portion.
And Mesaulius served them bread — a man the swineherd\nhad got for himself, alone, while his master was away,
without his mistress, without old Laertes:
he had bought him from the Taphians with goods of his own.
And their hands went out to the\ngood things spread before them.
But when they had put away desire for food and drink,\nMesaulius took away the bread; and they, filled
full of bread and meat, bestirred themselves for bed.
And the night came on, foul,\nat the moon's dark, and Zeus rained
the whole night through, and the wet\nWest Wind blew big without ceasing.
Then Odysseus spoke among them, testing the swineherd —
whether he would strip off his own cloak and give it,
or urge it out of one of his companions,\nsince he cared for him so:
"Hear me now, Eumaeus, and all you other companions,
while I speak a word of boasting: it is the crazing wine
that commands me — wine,\nthat sets even the deep-minded singing
and giggling softly, and stirs him up to dance,\nand tosses out many a word better left unspoken.
Still, since I have blurted once, I will hide nothing.
Would I were young, and my strength stood firm in me,
as on the day we laid our ambush and led it under Troy.
Odysseus led, and Atreus' son Menelaus, and with them\nI was third in command: they asked it themselves.
When we had come up to the city and the steep wall,\nwe lay around the town in the dense brushwood,
crouched under our arms among the reeds and marsh-grass,
and a foul night came on, the North Wind dropping down,
freezing; and snow came falling on us like hoarfrost,\nbitter cold, and ice crusted thick on the shields.
Then all the others had their cloaks and tunics,
and slept at their ease,\nshoulders wrapped in their shields;
but I had left my cloak behind with my companions —\nfool that I was — never thinking I would freeze:
I had come with only my shield and my shining waist-guard.
But in the night's third watch,\nwhen the stars had crossed their height,
then I spoke to Odysseus — he was there beside me —
nudging him with my elbow; and he listened on the instant:
'Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus of the many devices,\nI shall not be among the living long: this cold
is killing me. I have no cloak. Some power tricked\nme into a single tunic. And now there is no way out.'
So I spoke; and he then held this plan in his heart —\nsuch a man he was for counsel, and for fighting —
and speaking low, close in my ear, he said:
'Quiet now, lest some other Achaean hear you.'
Then he propped his head on his elbow and spoke out:
'Hear me, friends. A divine dream came to me in my sleep.
We have come out too far from the ships. Let someone go
and tell Atreus' son Agamemnon, shepherd of the people,\nto send more men from the ships to join us here.'
So he spoke; and up jumped Thoas, Andraemon's son,\nfast, and flung off his purple cloak,
and set off running for the ships.\nAnd I, in that man's garment,
lay glad until Dawn shone on her golden throne.
Would I were young like that now,\nand my strength stood firm:
then someone in this steading\nmight give a swineherd's cloak —
both ways at once: in kindness,\nand in respect for a good man.
As it is, they scorn me for the foul clothes on my skin."
And you answered him, Eumaeus the swineherd:
"Old man — that is a blameless fable you have told:
not one word of it off the measure;\nnothing said without its profit.
So you shall not lack for clothing, nor for anything\nelse that is owed a hard-worn suppliant when he comes —
tonight. But at dawn you will knock\nabout in those rags of yours again:
for there are not many cloaks here, or changes\nof tunic, to put on — one only for each man.
But when the dear son of Odysseus comes,\nhe will give you clothing himself, a cloak and a tunic,

So speaking he sprang up and set a bed for him close\nby the fire, and threw on it skins of sheep and goats.
There Odysseus lay down; and over\nhim the swineherd threw a cloak,
thick-woven and big, that he kept by him for a change\nof clothing, to put on when some terrible storm arose.
So Odysseus slept there, and beside him slept the\nyoung men. But the swineherd — a bed in that place
did not please him, to sleep apart from his swine;\nhe armed himself to go outside. And Odysseus was glad
that he took such care of his\nsubstance while he was far away.
First he slung his sharp sword over his sturdy shoulders,
then wrapped himself in a\nwind-breaking cloak, thick-woven,
and took up the fleece of a big well-fattened goat,\nand took his sharp javelin, to hold off dogs and men,
and went out to lie where the white-tusked boars slept,\nunder a hollow rock, in the lee of the North Wind.
